One Page Website for Coaches and Course Creators

By Marie Glow StudioUpdated September 23, 2026

A coach or course creator often needs a website that does one job: help a stranger understand what you offer, believe you can deliver it and take the next step. A one page website can do that well, and it is usually faster and cheaper than a multi-page build. It also has real limits, and knowing them before you start saves you from buying the wrong thing.

This guide is about the one page format specifically. If you are still weighing whether to build it yourself, the DIY versus professional website design post lays out the tradeoffs, and the small business website essentials post covers what every site needs.

What a one page site is good at

A single page works when your offer is simple enough to explain in one scroll. That describes many coaches (one main program or a short list of services), and many course creators (one course and a way to join the waitlist). A single page keeps the visitor moving down one path, which removes the navigation maze that pulls people away from the thing you want them to do.

The four sections every coaching one pager needs

1. The offer, stated plainly

Lead with who it is for, the problem you help with and what working with you involves. Skip the mission statement. A visitor should be able to finish the top of the page and say, "This is for someone like me." List what is included in the program or course, and what the format is (one to one, group, self paced).

2. Proof

Proof beats promises. Use only what is real and that you have permission to share: testimonials from actual clients, your credentials, the number of people you have worked with if you can state it accurately, or a short account of your own path. If you are just starting and have none of these, be honest about it and use your story and your method instead. Never invent a result to fill the space.

3. An opt-in

Not everyone is ready to book today. A free guide, checklist or short email series gives cautious visitors a low-pressure next step and gives you a way to follow up. Pick something small that solves one specific problem, and say what they get and how often you will email. The lead magnet ideas post has starting points, even though it is written for product businesses, and growing an email list from scratch covers what to do after someone signs up.

4. One clear way to book or get in touch

Choose a single primary action, such as booking a call or sending a message, and repeat it at the top, the middle and the bottom of the page. The Website Starter includes a contact section with social links. If you also want an embedded booking or email form from another service, confirm that scope before you buy, because it is not in the listed inclusions.

What a one page site cannot do

Be clear about the limits so you are not surprised later:

  • It cannot sell products. The Website Starter is a static one page site, not Shopify and not e-commerce. There is no cart or checkout.
  • It cannot hold a blog or a deep library. Everything lives on one page, so there is little room for content that ranks for many different searches.
  • It cannot serve several audiences well. If you have three separate offers for three different people, one scroll gets crowded fast.

If you sell downloads or physical items alongside your coaching, the Shopify website guide for digital product sellers covers the store side.

When to outgrow it

Consider moving up when you notice any of these: you want to sell products or courses directly on your own site, you have more offers than one page can present clearly, you want a blog, or you keep wishing you could send different visitors to different pages. Extra pages on the Website Starter are $79 each, which is a reasonable bridge for a few more pages. If you need a store, the Complete Website and Brand Identity is the route, and $100 of what you paid for the Starter is credited toward it if you upgrade within 6 months.

Bring people to the page

A page does nothing without visitors. Pinterest can be a steady source for coaches, because people search there for planning, habits and business help. See Pinterest marketing for coaches and course creators for how that works.

Frequently asked questions

What should a one page website for a coach include?

A coaching one pager should include a plain statement of the offer and who it is for, real proof such as testimonials or credentials, an opt-in for visitors who are not ready to book, and one clear way to book or get in touch, repeated down the page.

Can a one page website sell my course?

Not directly. The Website Starter is a static one page site and is not e-commerce, so it has no cart or checkout. It can present the course and point people to a waitlist or contact option, and a store needs a different setup.

When should a coach move from a one page site to a bigger website?

Move up when you want to sell directly on your own site, when you have more offers than one page can present clearly, or when you want a blog or separate pages for different audiences. Extra pages on the Website Starter are $79 each.

The Website Starter is delivered in 5 business days from a completed intake form, or the revision round is free. It costs $249 one-time and includes one revision round.
